# Network protocols are vulnerable to attacks

- All protocols have an attack surface
- Attack surface is the set of vulnerabilities
- Hackers exploit these vulnerabilities
- Protocol designers must anticipate attacks

## Network Protocol Lifecycle

::: {.fragment style="margin-top: -0.5em; font-size: 0.725em;"}

- **Design Protocol**
  - Define rules for communication
  - Specify message structure and semantics

- **Discover Vulnerability**
  - Identify security weaknesses
  - Analyze attack vectors

- **Patch Protocol**
  - Implement security fixes
  - Update protocol specifications

- **Repeat Process**
  - Continuously monitor for new threats
  - Iterate to enhance protocol security

:::

# What are some common attacks on computer networking protocol?

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 0.9em; margin-top: -0.5em;"}

- Interception attacks
- Network layer attacks
- Internet layer attacks
- Name-resolution attacks
- Web-based attacks

:::

## Verifying a Server Certificate

```text
$ openssl s_client -connect www.securitysynapse.org:443 \
    -servername www.securitysynapse.org
Connecting to 104.21.20.61
depth=2 C=US, O=Google Trust Services LLC, CN=GTS Root R4
verify return:1
depth=1 C=US, O=Google Trust Services, CN=WE1
verify return:1
depth=0 CN=securitysynapse.org
verify return:1
...
Verify return code: 0 (ok)
```

::: {.fragment .fade style="margin-top: 0.15em; font-size: 0.85em;"}

- The client verifies a certificate chain up to a trusted root server
- `Verify return code: 0 (ok)` proves the server's identity
- A MITM cannot present a trusted certificate for the same name
- `-servername` (SNI) requests the certificate for the chosen host

:::

## Replays and One-Time Passwords

::: {.incremental style="margin-top: -0.25em; font-size: 0.95em;"}

- **Replay Attacks**
  - Attacker intercepts and reuses valid data
  - Exploits repeated transmission
  - Compromises authentication

- **Thwarting with One-Time Passwords (OTPs)**
  - Unique password for each session
  - Valid for a single use only
  - Prevents reuse of intercepted data

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 0.85em; margin-top: -0.25em;"}

{{< iconify fa6-solid lightbulb >}} **OTPs enhance security and data integrity and thwart replay attacks!**

:::

## Attacking the MAC Address

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=50%}

::: {.incremental style="margin-top: -0.25em; font-size: 0.925em;"}

- **MAC Spoofing/Cloning**
  - Attacker changes a device's MAC address
  - Now possible to bypass network access controls
  - Enables the impersonation of legitimate devices

:::

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

::: {.incremental style="margin-top: -0.25em; font-size: 0.925em;"}

- **MAC Flooding**
  - Switches track MAC to IP address mapping
  - Overloads the switch with fake MAC addresses
  - Compromises network performance

:::

:::

::::

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 0.85em; margin-top: -0.35em;"}

- Attack performed at the network layer
- Exploits the inherent weaknesses of MAC addresses
- **How can we mitigate this type of attack?**

:::

## Mitigating the MAC Address Attacks

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 0.825em; margin-top: 0.05em;"}

- **Port Security**
  - Configure switch ports to allow only specific MAC addresses
  - Limit the number of MAC addresses per port
  - Use sticky MAC addresses to learn and restrict MAC addresses

- **802.1X Authentication**
  - Network access controls to authenticate devices before network access
  - Ensure that only authorized devices can connect to the network

- **VLAN Segmentation**
  - Segment the network into smaller VLANs
  - Limit the broadcast domain and reduce the impact of MAC spoofing

:::

## Inspecting the MAC and ARP Layer

```text
$ ip -brief link | awk '{print $1, $3}'
lo 00:00:00:00:00:00
wlp1s0 aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01
enp103s0 aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:02

$ ip neigh
172.16.0.1   dev enp103s0 lladdr aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:03 REACHABLE
172.16.0.7   dev enp103s0 FAILED
172.16.0.9   dev enp103s0 lladdr aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:04 STALE
172.16.0.21  dev wlp1s0   lladdr aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:05 STALE
```

::: {.fragment .fade style="margin-top: 0.15em; font-size: 0.825em;"}

- `ip -brief link` shows each interface and its `ether` (MAC) address
- `ip neigh` is the ARP cache of trusted IP-to-MAC bindings
- Spoofing or poisoning one binding redirects traffic to the attacker
- Port security, 802.1X, and VLANs limit how far a bad binding spreads
- What are all the output codes for the `ip neigh` command?

:::

## IP Spoofing

::: {.fragment style="margin-top: -0.5em; font-size: 0.8em;"}

- **Inherent Insecurity**
  - IP was not designed with security
  - Easy to forge IP addresses

- **Protocol Limitations**
  - No built-in authentication
  - No integrity checks

- **IPSec Solution**
  - Adds security to IP layer
  - Provides authentication and encryption

- **Layered Security**
  - Secure solutions needed at multiple layers

:::

# Combine application and transport layer security to achieve a network that is more secure overall! *Nice!* {transition="convex"}

## DNS Cache Poisoning

::: {.incremental style="margin-top: -0.5em; font-size: 0.8em;"}

- **Attack Overview**
  - Attacker corrupts DNS cache
  - Redirects users to malicious sites

- **Vulnerability**
  - Exploits lack of DNS query validation
  - Alters DNS responses

- **Consequences**
  - Phishing attacks
  - Data theft

- **Mitigation**
  - Use DNSSEC for validation!

:::

## Validating DNS with DNSSEC

```text
$ dig +dnssec @1.1.1.1 cloudflare.com A
;; flags: qr rd ra ad; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 3, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1
;; ANSWER SECTION:
cloudflare.com. 300 IN A 104.16.132.229
cloudflare.com. 300 IN A 104.16.133.229
cloudflare.com. 300 IN RRSIG A 13 2 300 ... B9g8fuuo...G5w==
$ dig +dnssec @1.1.1.1 securitysynapse.org A
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 2, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1
;; ANSWER SECTION:
securitysynapse.org. 300 IN A 172.67.191.211
securitysynapse.org. 300 IN A 104.21.20.61
```

::: {.fragment .fade style="margin-top: 0.15em; font-size: 0.85em;"}

- `@1.1.1.1` pins a resolver that validates DNSSEC
- `+dnssec` sets the DO bit, asking for the `RRSIG` records
- `ad` (authenticated data) means the resolver verified the signatures
- `securitysynapse.org` is unsigned: no `ad` and no `RRSIG`

:::

## DNSSEC on Additional Web Sites

```text
$ dig +dnssec @1.1.1.1 whitehouse.gov A +noall +comments +answer
;; flags: qr rd ra ad; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 2, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1
;; ANSWER SECTION:
whitehouse.gov. 196 IN A 192.0.66.51
whitehouse.gov. 196 IN RRSIG A 13 2 300 ... oyDXuKLq...Q==
$ for d in ietf.org nist.gov google.com; do \
>   dig +dnssec @1.1.1.1 "$d" A +noall +comments \
>     | grep -qE "flags:.* ad;" && echo "$d signed" \
>     || echo "$d unsigned"; done
ietf.org signed
nist.gov signed
google.com unsigned
```

::: {.fragment .fade style="margin-top: 0.1em; font-size: 0.85em;"}

- `whitehouse.gov` is signed: `ad` plus a covering `RRSIG`
- Other signed sites: `ietf.org`, `nist.gov`, `ripe.net`, `iana.org`
- `google.com` is not signed, so no validating resolver sets `ad`
- Signing is the zone owner's choice; validation is the resolver's job

:::

# Let's talk about prominent types of injection attacks at the application layer

- {{< iconify fa6-solid database >}} Cross-site scripting attacks
- {{< iconify fa6-solid globe >}} SQL injection attacks

## Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) {transition="convex"}

::: {.incremental style="margin-top: -0.5em; font-size: 0.8em;"}

- **Attack Overview**
  - Attacker injects malicious scripts
  - Executes in user's browser

- **Vulnerability**
  - Poor input validation
  - Inadequate output encoding

- **Consequences**
  - Data theft
  - Session hijacking

- **Mitigation**
  - Validate and sanitize inputs

:::

## SQL Injection Attacks {transition="convex"}

::: {.fragment style="margin-top: -0.5em; font-size: 0.8em;"}

- **Attack Overview**
  - Attacker injects malicious SQL queries
  - Executes in the database

- **Vulnerability**
  - Poor input validation
  - Directly embedding user input in SQL queries

- **Consequences**
  - Data leakage
  - Unauthorized data modification

- **Mitigation**
  - Use prepared statements and validate and sanitize inputs

:::

# Remote Code Execution

- Gives attacker ability to run arbitrary code
- Start a shell with administrative privileges
- Gains full control of the system, its users, and data
- The "launching pad" for attacks like a denial of service

::: {.fragment .fade .boxed-content style="margin-top: .20em; font-size: 0.875em;"}

{{< iconify fa6-solid diagram-project >}} The buffer overflow attack is a common
method for achieving remote code execution! What is it? How can we prevent this
attack?

:::

## Making Memory Harder to Predict

```text
$ cat overflow.py
import ctypes
libc = ctypes.CDLL(None)
buf = ctypes.create_string_buffer(16)
print(f"buf at {ctypes.addressof(buf):#x}")
libc.strcpy(buf, b"A" * 64)   # overflows the 16-byte buffer!
$ python3 overflow.py; python3 overflow.py
buf at 0x72711c13e2c0
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
buf at 0x737581b3e2c0
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
$ sysctl kernel.randomize_va_space
kernel.randomize_va_space = 2
```

::: {.fragment .fade style="margin-top: 0.1em; font-size: 0.78em;"}

- `strcpy` ignores the 16-byte size and corrupts adjacent memory
- `ctypes` reaches the real C `strcpy`, so this is a C overflow, not a Python bug
- `randomize_va_space = 2` shows use of OS's ASLR, not a Python feature
- An exploit cannot hard-code the address, which raises the cost of RCE

:::

## Privilege Escalation

::: {.fragment style="margin-top: -.25em; font-size: 0.75em;"}

- **Details about the attack**
  - Gain access to protected resources
  - Example: [CVE-2021-4034](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2021-4034) in Linux `pkexec`
  - Exploit gives regular user a root shell

:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top: -.65em; font-size: 0.75em;"}

- **Methods of privilege escalation**
  - Credential exploitation
  - Vulnerabilities or misconfigurations
  - Social engineering

:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top: -.65em; font-size: 0.75em;"}

- **Privilege escalation types**
  - *Horizontal*: move between user accounts
  - *Vertical*: gain higher-level access (e.g., user to admin)

:::

## Denial of Service (DoS)

::: {.fragment style="margin-top: -.25em; font-size: 0.75em;"}

- **DoS Attack**
  - Overwhelm system with requests
  - DDoS means multiple machines work together

:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top: -.65em; font-size: 0.75em;"}

- **Types of DoS Attacks**
  - SYN Floods: unfinished handshakes
  - ICMP Floods: pinging to overwhelm
  - Buffer Overflows: unexpected data

:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top: -.65em; font-size: 0.75em;"}

- **Prevention**
  - SYN cookies for SYN Floods
  - Rate limit ICMP packets
  - Secure software design

:::

## What Is a SYN Flood?

::: {.incremental style="margin-top: -0.6em; font-size: 0.775em;"}

- **Normal TCP handshake**
  - Client sends `SYN`; server replies `SYN-ACK`
  - Client's `ACK` completes the connection

- **SYN flood attack**
  - Attacker floods `SYN`s, often spoofed
  - The final `ACK` never arrives

- **The impact**
  - Half-open entries exhaust the backlog
  - Legitimate clients are refused service

:::

::: {.fragment .fade .boxed-content style="margin-top: -0.25em; font-size: 0.775em;"}

{{< iconify fa6-solid lightbulb >}} **Availability** attack: **unfinished**
handshakes exhaust the server and deny service

:::

## Defending Against SYN Floods

```text
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1

$ ss -s
Total: 1391
TCP:   142 (estab 105, closed 15, orphaned 0, timewait 14)

Transport Total     IP        IPv6
RAW       1         0         1
UDP       5         5         0
TCP       127       126       1
INET      133       131       2
FRAG      0         0         0

```

::: {.fragment .fade style="margin-top: 0.15em; font-size: 0.75em;"}

- This `ss -s` output is a **baseline**: no flood is in progress
- `tcp_syncookies = 1` answers a `SYN` without reserving memory
- The `SYN-ACK` carries a cookie, checked when the real `ACK` returns
- Fake `SYN`s cost almost nothing, so real clients still get in

:::

# Can we build a network monitoring tool?

- Client sends messages to server
- Server receives messages from clients
- Intercept network communication
- Client and server are not aware!

## Network Monitoring Tool

::: {.incremental style="margin-top: -.65em; font-size: 0.8em;"}

- Let's build a client and a server and intercept network communication!

- `networkmonitor` start a process in one of these modes:
  - **Client and Server Protocols**:
    - **Socket Server**: Start a server using sockets
    - **Socket Client**: Start a client using sockets
    - **XML-RPC Server**: Start a server using XML-RPC
    - **XML-RPC Client**: Start a client using XML-RPC
  - **Interception Mechanisms**:
    - **Socket Interception**: Intercept socket network communication
    - **XML-RPC Interception**: Intercept XML-RPC network communication

- See the course web site's project description for more details!

:::
